scenario: AITA for not buying my siblings gifts because they refuse to do a secret Santa? | I have a bunch of siblings, all grown adults, and buying gifts for everyone including parents, partners, and kids is out of control. While I am financially okish, I just can't afford it. Also, neither can my parents and previous years have resulted in my mom being depressed and stressed trying to buy everyone something. Last year, after a some resistance, we agreed to do a secret santa and it went pretty well. Or so I thought. This year 1 sibling threw a fit about doing it. She said she doesn't like "putting rules on holidays" and it's not fair. As a side note, she and our younger siblings rarely buy anyone anything. Last year was the 1st time everyone brought something. Another sibling, who is hosting Christmas, sided with her and said that we won't do a secret Santa but that you don't have to bring gifts if you don't want to. Am an asshole if I don't buy my siblings gifts? I love my family but I can't afford it this year. I was going to get nieces and nephews gifts but that's it.

prediction.raw: 0 You are not the asshole in this scenario. It's completely reasonable to set boundaries and prioritize your financial well-being, especially when it comes to a large family with many members. The fact that you suggested a Secret Santa last year and it worked well, but some siblings refused to participate this year, is not your problem. It's also unfair to expect you to bear the financial burden of buying gifts for everyone when others are not contributing equally. It's great that you're considering getting gifts for your nieces and nephews, as they are likely to appreciate the thought and excitement of receiving presents. However, it's perfectly fine to draw the line at buying gifts for your adult siblings, especially when you've already communicated your financial concerns and suggested a more manageable alternative. Your siblings' refusal to participate in a Secret Santa and their expectation that you should still buy gifts for them is unreasonable and entitled. It's not about "putting rules on holidays," but about finding a way to make gift-giving sustainable and enjoyable for everyone involved. By setting boundaries and prioritizing your own financial well-being, you're taking care of yourself and avoiding unnecessary stress and financial strain.
